text: Every tutorial says a qubit in superposition is 'both 0 and 1 at the same time,' and almost every tutorial leaves you with the wrong mental model. Superposition isn't secret, hidden information about which value the qubit really has — it's a physical fact you can actually test, and the test is interference.

Here's the explanation almost everyone reaches for first: the qubit is really 0 or really 1, nature just hasn't decided yet, or we don't know which, so we describe it with 50/50 odds until we look. That's a classical probabilistic mixture — the uncertainty lives in your head, not the object, exactly like a coin spinning in the air before it lands. The trouble is, this picture makes a hard, testable prediction: running the qubit through two operations in a row should just be two independent draws from the same hidden fact. Quantum mechanics violates that prediction every time.

Recall the Hadamard gate sends ket-zero to ket-plus. Apply Hadamard a second time, to ket-plus itself, and you get back exactly ket-zero — not approximately, not usually, but exactly, every single time, since H times H equals the identity. If ket-plus really meant secretly 0 or secretly 1 with fixed odds, a second operation should just combine with that hidden value the way a second coin flip does — some spread of outcomes, not a guaranteed, certain return. A classical mixture has no mechanism to make two 50/50 steps cancel into one sure outcome. But that's exactly what happens.

That cancel-and-reinforce behavior is called interference, and it's the real signature of superposition. Amplitudes are numbers that can effectively point in different directions, and when two paths contribute to the same outcome, their amplitudes add together before you square them into a probability. Same direction, and they constructively interfere and reinforce; opposite directions, and they destructively interfere and cancel, even all the way to zero. Plain probabilities can never do this — they're non-negative numbers that only add, never cancel.

This isn't a philosophical footnote — it's the entire resource quantum algorithms spend their effort exploiting. A circuit is a carefully engineered sequence of gates designed to make wrong-answer amplitudes destructively interfere toward zero, while the correct answer's amplitude constructively interferes and grows. If superposition were just classical hidden ignorance, there'd be nothing to interfere, and quantum computers would have no advantage over flipping coins.
Next lesson shows exactly what happens when you finally look at a qubit — how the Born rule turns these amplitudes into the probabilities you actually observe.
